summary: Describes content splicing for RTP sessions, where part of a main media stream is replaced with other content for a while, such as a local advertisement replacing a national one. The memo covers the mechanisms and signaling involved. It is informational.

eli5.summary: During a TV show, the usual advert is swapped for one from your town, then the show carries on. This explains how that swap works over the internet.

questions: how does rtp content splicing work
how to insert local ads into a media stream
how does local ad insertion work
subtitle: Replacing parts of streaming video with other content

tldr.problem: When streaming video over RTP, broadcasters often need to insert local content into a main stream, like replacing a national advertisement with a local one. The incoming main stream and the substitutive stream may have different lengths and packet counts due to different codecs, requiring RTP header adjustments.
tldr.mechanism: A splicer intermediary acts as an RTP mixer, receiving both the main and substitutive content streams, selecting which one to send to receivers based on timing signals, and rewriting RTP headers (sequence number and timestamp) to maintain consistency. The mixer also handles RTCP control messages between senders and receivers, mapping them between the two content sources.
tldr.outcome: Seamless splicing at the RTP layer is possible using standard RFC 3550 tools without requiring protocol extensions or changes to endpoints. Cable TV, video conferencing, and streaming services can insert ads or other content transparently.

today: RFC 6828 is informational and remains the primary reference for RTP-layer content splicing. While MPEG-based standards like SCTE 35 are widely used in traditional broadcast and cable, the RTP approach described here is relevant for internet-delivered video services and any RTP-based streaming where content insertion is needed.

sections.title: What Is Content Splicing
sections.content:
Content splicing is replacing part of a multimedia stream with different content for a period of time, then resuming the original stream. The classic use case is local advertisement insertion in cable television: a network broadcast includes national advertisements, but a cable operator replaces them with local advertisements before sending the stream to subscribers. Other applications include inserting recorded video into a video conference, implementing a playlist server that stitches pieces of video together, or temporarily replacing a live feed with a backup recording during a technical problem.

Cable TV systems have standardized splicing for MPEG2 streams through standards like SCTE 30 and SCTE 35. When multimedia content is delivered over the internet using RTP (Real-Time Transport Protocol), the same splicing is needed but at the RTP layer. The challenge is that the main content and the substitutive content may use different video codecs, different bitrates, and different numbers of RTP packets to encode the same time duration. An intermediary splicer must rewrite RTP headers to hide these differences from the receiver.
sections.eli5: A TV company broadcasts a show with national ads. The cable company's box intercepts the signal, replaces the national ad with a local one, and sends everything to your TV. The box has to make sure your TV player does not notice the switch or get confused about what comes next.

sections.title: How the Splicer Works
sections.content:
The splicer is a network intermediary that receives two RTP streams: the main RTP stream (the content being broadcast) and a substitutive RTP stream (the replacement content). The splicer forwards one stream or the other to receivers at any given time, but never both.

When a splicing-in point is reached (typically at the boundary between two video frames, to avoid mid-frame cuts), the splicer switches from forwarding main content to forwarding substitutive content. While substitutive content is active, the splicer extracts the payload data from the substitutive stream and repackages it in RTP packets using its own source identifier (SSRC) and its own sequence number space. When a splicing-out point is reached, the splicer switches back to forwarding main content.

From the receiver's perspective, all packets come from a single source (the splicer), with a continuous sequence number, so it appears as one unbroken stream. The receiver does not know that some packets contain substitutive content; it simply decodes and plays everything that arrives. The mechanism for determining when to splice (what triggers splicing-in and splicing-out) is outside the scope of this RFC; in practice, a control system outside the RTP flow signals the splicer when to switch.
sections.eli5: The splicer sits between the main stream and the receiver. It watches both streams and picks which one to send onward. When the ad should start, it switches to the ad stream. When the ad should end, it switches back. It rewrites the packet numbers so the receiver thinks it is all one stream.

sections.title: Handling Control Messages
sections.content:
RTP streams are accompanied by RTCP (Real-Time Control Protocol) messages that carry feedback between senders and receivers: packet loss reports, jitter measurements, and other performance metrics. The splicer must handle RTCP carefully because a receiver's RTCP report may span multiple content sources.

If an RTCP report entirely covers a time period when main content was sent, the splicer forwards the report to the main sender with SSRC and sequence numbers mapped back to the main stream's identifiers. If it entirely covers substitutive content, the report goes to the substitutive sender instead. If an RTCP report spans a splicing point (covering both main and substitutive content), the splicer must split it into two reports, each with the correct source and sequence numbers, and send them to the respective senders.

The splicer may also generate its own RTCP reports to inform the main sender and substitutive sender of the reception quality of their streams as seen by the mixer itself (before splicing), separate from the reception quality seen by the downstream receiver. If substitutive content comes from a local media file rather than a live RTP stream, the splicer terminates RTCP for that source without forwarding it.
sections.eli5: When the receiver complains that packets are getting lost, the splicer has to figure out: was it during the main show or during the ad? Then it tells the right sender about the problem, using the right packet numbers so the sender understands.

sections.title: Handling Length Mismatches
sections.content:
A practical challenge is that substitutive content may not have the exact same duration as the main content it replaces. If the substitutive content is shorter than the gap in the main stream, there will be a gap in the output: sequence numbers remain continuous, but the RTP timestamp jumps unexpectedly. The receiver has nothing to play during this gap, resulting in silence or a frozen frame. The mixer can sometimes adjust splice points or request that substitutive content be extended, but this is complex.

If the substitutive content is longer than the reserved gap, it will overlap with the resumption of the main stream. A simple approach is for the mixer to abruptly terminate splicing and switch back to main content, which may cause stuttering or a jump in playback. Alternatively, the mixer could transcode the substitutive content to play at a faster rate to fit the allocated duration, but this is codec-specific and computationally expensive. The best practice is for the content provider to ensure that substitutive content has nearly the same duration as the main content it replaces.
sections.eli5: If the ad is shorter than the time slot for ads, there is silence. If the ad is longer, the show gets cut off. The trick is to measure carefully beforehand and make sure the ad is almost exactly the right length.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The splicer imposes overhead on the mixer, which must rewrite RTP headers and RTCP messages even when no splicing is active. The mixer uses its own SSRC and sequence number space for all output packets, ensuring that the receiver always sees a single source and continuous packet numbering. When serving multiple main streams simultaneously, the overhead multiplies.

A security concern: if the splicer does not include contributing source (CSRC) information in output RTP packets (which is necessary to hide splicing from the receiver), RTP loop-detection mechanisms fail. Without CSRC lists, the system cannot detect if packets loop back to an upstream node, which could cause a denial-of-service by flooding the network. Operators must use non-RTP means (network topology monitoring, configuration validation) to detect and prevent loops.

The splicer also breaks end-to-end security. If the RTP stream is encrypted (using SRTP), the splicer must decrypt incoming packets to read the payload, splice in new content, and re-encrypt outgoing packets. This requires the splicer to be in the security context with both the main sender and the substitutive sender, treating it as a trusted node. It cannot maintain source authentication from the original sender to the receiver; instead, security is between the splicer and receiver, and between each sender and the splicer.
sections.eli5: The box doing the splicing has to work hard, rewriting packets even when not splicing. If the streams are encrypted, the box has to decrypt them, do the swap, and encrypt again—so it has to be trusted. And if packets somehow loop back, bad things happen.
